name: American art pottery
region: Cincinnati, Boston and New Orleans, United States
summary: Art pottery from American potteries after 1880. Rookwood painted slip under a clear glaze, and Grueby made thick matt green glazes for vases with leaf forms.

philosophy.core_thesis: A pottery of artists can make a vase a painting or a leaf: one line paints in slip under glaze, and the other line builds the form in matt colour.
design_principles: Paint the design in coloured slip on damp clay, so that the colours blend like a watercolour.
Cover the painted piece with a clear glossy glaze, the Standard glaze, and fire it once.
Grade the ground from dark brown to orange, olive or yellow with an atomiser spray.
Paint one flower, fish or portrait on each vase; the painter signs with a monogram.
For a matt line, use a thick glaze of 1 to 2 mm in a single colour, green above all.
Mould the leaf and the stem in the wall, and make the glaze pool in the hollows.
Mark each piece on the base with a stamp, a date code and a shape number.
Fire in oxidation at about 1100 to 1250 °C for earthenware and 1250 °C for stoneware.
anti_patterns: A white body with a printed transfer pattern
Glossy flat colour with no tone
A mark that is missing or only a number

form.shape: Tall vases, bottle vases, lidded jars and planters, with a full belly, a narrow neck and plain, strong lines.
form.profile: A swelling curve from a narrow foot to the shoulder; leaf-moulded wall pieces have vertical ribs that rise to the neck.
form.foot_and_rim: A small flat foot with a stamped mark; the rim is a plain or a thick rolled lip.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 50 cm; the wall is 5 to 9 mm thick.
rules: Keep the form simple, so that the painting or the glaze is the surface.
Mould the ribs and leaves in the wall for the matt pieces.
Stamp the base with the pottery mark and the shape number.

bodies.rule: Use a local red or buff clay that takes slip and a thick glaze. The body must be sturdy enough to carry a matt glaze of 1 to 2 mm.

methods: jiggering and moulding of repeat shapes
carving and incising in leather-hard clay
forming.joins: The foot and the neck are thrown in one piece; handles are pulled and joined by hand.
forming.details: A stamped pottery mark, a date code, the initials of the decorator, and a glaze that pools in the hollows.

glaze.pattern: A flower, a fish, a landscape or a portrait on a dark ground in the Standard line; a plain leaf and a single matt green in the Grueby line.
glaze.gloss: Standard glaze 70 to 90 GU; matt glaze 5 to 20 GU.
glaze.wear: Standard glaze crazes with age; matt glaze keeps a velvet feel and can show finger marks.

palette.strategy: A tonal ground from dark brown to orange or yellow, with soft painted flowers; or a single matt green.

firing.kiln: A coal-fired round-down kiln; later a gas kiln.
processes: biscuit firing of the moulded and thrown body
slip painting and spraying of the ground
dipping or spraying of the clear glaze
firing.scale: Some 50 decorators at the largest pottery in the 1890s; thousands of pieces each year, each painted by hand.
firing.signs: A pottery stamp, a decorator cipher, a date code, and a soft blend of slip colours under the glaze.

pieces.form: Tall vase with a painted orange flower on a dark ground, Standard glaze
Bottle vase with a thick matt green glaze and moulded leaf ribs
Squat jar with a lid, carved lotus leaves and a matt glaze
Round planter with a coloured gloss glaze and a band of moulded flowers
Baluster vase with an Indian portrait on a smoky ground

positive: dark brown to orange blended ground

canonical_works.work: Standard glaze vase with an Iris
Leaf and flower vase in matt green

evidence.title: Grueby Faience Company vase, matt glaze
Grueby Pottery vase, Cleveland Museum of Art 1972.1064

emotion.target_response: A feeling of quiet pride in a local craft: the viewer sees a soft flower or a leaf in rich colour and sees the maker at work.

use_cases: a hand-painted vase for a Craftsman interior
a museum label on American art pottery
avoid_when: the brief needs a printed pattern
the brief needs wild, flowing curves

modifiers.how: Replace the plain form with a whiplash curve and use a flambé or crystalline glaze.
Use a stoneware or tin-glazed body and paint in lustre; keep the visible hand.
